summary: The frozen history test rejected every pre-registered stock rule: each beat only a small share of random baskets from the same list, and holding every name equally beat every rule and the core. Setup checks and past strength have shown no edge here. The market's mood turned stressed, and every name fell on the latest day. All five calls stay neutral with low conviction. Nothing here is expected to beat the index; real money stays in the whole-market plan.
eli5: Everyone in the race slowed down on the latest day, and the whole field looks tired. The brain does not guess which runner gets going again, because guessing did no better than luck before. It watches with pretend money, and the family's real money keeps going into the whole-market basket every week.
letter:
Dear family,

First, real money. Nothing to do today, and nothing to sell. The market's mood has turned stressed, which feels worse than it usually is. Next week's buy of the whole-market fund goes in as always; a weak patch means the same amount buys a bit more. Money we may need soon stays safe.

Second, the pretend game. Every stock rule we wrote down in advance lost to baskets picked at random from the same list, so our stock calls stay neutral. The weekly bet game stands at two weeks won and one lost, and this week's bet is a little behind so far.

Third, a lesson. A day ago Microsoft and Apple jumped and Alphabet bounced; today all of them gave some of it back. Watching one day at a time makes the market feel like a storm. Looked at by the year, it is weather.

Fourth, what would change our minds: a rule that beats random picks on history and then keeps a paper record ahead of the whole market for at least half a year. Until then we stay patient.

With care, the brain

bets.why: This week's bet was already placed and is repeated unchanged: names above their trend passing every setup check, against names below their trend whose checklist leaned down. No rule like this has beaten luck, so it is a learning bet only.

pick.thesis: Alphabet gave back its bounce on the latest day and sits far below its high for the year and below its fifty-day average, behind the benchmark on every window; the checklist now reads mixed. Its filing shows strong growth but thin free cash flow. The house rule says never to buy only because a stock fell a lot, and no tested rule shows that deep falls on this list bounce back. Berkshire's disclosed book holds it and is behind; that record is the firm's and too thin to count. Neutral and low, unchanged.
